courses.repertoire: Giuoco Pianissimo: c3, d3, and a slow build-up
courses.summary: Build with c3 and d3, castle, bring the queen's knight to g3, and break with d4 when ready.
overview: One plan against almost everything: c3 and d3, castle, Re1 and h3, and the knight route b1-d2-f1-g3. Play d4 only when it gains something.
Black's third move decides the chapter: 3...Bc5 comes up in about 40% of your games, and 3...Nf6 in about 30%.
Against 3...Nf6, play 4.d3, not 4.Ng5 or 4.Nc3: e4 stays protected, and you skip the Fried Liver theory and the fork trick.
Keep the Italian bishop. Drop it back to b3 or c2 before ...Na5 or ...b5 can trade it off.
The pin ...Bg4 is harmless here: ask the bishop with h3, guard f3 with Nbd2, and chase it with Ng3 and Nh4.
f7 is Black's weak point. If Black shuts in the f8 bishop with ...d6 and then plays ...Nf6, Ng5 hits f7 at once.

courses.summary: Mirror White's slow setup, keep the bishop with ...a6 and ...Ba7, and know how to meet d4 and the Evans Gambit.
overview: Play 3...Bc5, then ...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. On a7 the bishop survives d4 and b4 and still aims at f2.
In more than half of your games White builds slowly with c3 and d3, or castles first. Mirror the setup: castle, ...h6 to keep White's pieces off g5, ...Re8, then ...Be6 and ...d5.
Don't rush ...d5. Played before you've developed, it lets White's queen join the bishop against d5 and f7 with Qb3.
Against the Center attack (4.c3 and 5.d4), take on d4, check on b4, and free your game with ...d5.
The Møller Attack, 7.Nc3, comes up often: take on e4, because the pin on c3 makes it safe.
Against the Evans Gambit (4.b4), take the pawn, retreat to a5, and give it back with ...d5 at the right moment.

courses.repertoire: Advance (Short system), plus the Two Knights and the Fantasy
courses.summary: Gain space with 3.e5, castle before anything sharp, and meet ...c5 calmly. The Two Knights and the Fantasy are trap-filled surprise weapons.
overview: Learn one system first. The Advance (3.e5) is the main weapon; the Two Knights (2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3) and the Fantasy (3.f3) are surprise weapons full of traps.
In the Advance, the pawn on e5 gains space and keeps Black's knight off f6. Develop calmly with Nf3, Be2 and O-O before anything sharp.
The main line, 3...Bf5 4.Nf3 e6, comes up in more than half of your Advance games.
Black's counterplay is ...c5 against d4, the base of your pawn chain. Guard d4 with Be3; against an early 3...c5, take with 4.dxc5.
In the Two Knights, wait before playing d4. Ask Black's bishop the question with h3 and take the bishop pair. After 4...Nf6, 5.Qe2 sets the smothered-mate trap.
In the Fantasy, the f-pawn holds e4. If Black takes, fxe4 gives you two center pawns and the half-open f-file, but your king is looser, so develop fast and castle.

courses.summary: Get the c8 bishop out before ...e6, hit d4 against the Advance, and know the traps in the Fantasy and Karpov lines.
overview: The idea of the Caro-Kann: support ...d5 with the c-pawn, and get the c8 bishop out before ...e6 shuts it in.

Learn three structures first: the Advance (3.e5), the Classical (3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2) and the Exchange (exd5 cxd5), which comes from both 2.d4 and 2.Nf3. Together they come up in more than half of your games.
Against the Advance (3.e5), hit the base of White's chain at once with 3...c5. Against 4.c3, take on d4 and pile up on it with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...Nf5.
Against 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2, take on e4 and play 4...Bf5. Answer h4 with ...h6, and trade the light-squared bishops calmly.
In the Exchange, develop with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...e6, then play for the minority attack with ...b5 and ...b4. Against the Panov's isolated d-pawn, blockade d5 and trade pieces.
Know the traps: in the Fantasy, 5.dxe5? runs into ...Qh4+; in the Karpov, 5.Qe2 Ngf6?? allows 6.Nd6 mate.

courses.repertoire: Advance (3.e5), with 6.a3 in the main line
courses.summary: Gain space with 3.e5, hold d4 with c3 and Nf3, and expand on the queenside with a3 and b4. The Milner-Barry Gambit is a trap-filled surprise weapon.
overview: Play 3.e5. The pawn takes f6 away from Black's king's knight and gives you space; Black answers 3...c5 in nine games out of ten.
Hold d4 with c3 and Nf3. Black's whole plan is pressure on that pawn with ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and a knight on f5.
The main line, 5...Qb6, comes up in a quarter of your games. Play 6.a3 and b4 to gain space; after 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, Nc3 and Na4 chase the queen.
Count the attackers before Black takes on d4. With your queen behind the pawn, ...Nxd4 just drops a piece; with your bishop on d3 in the way, Bb5+ wins Black's queen.
Against 5...Bd7, play 6.Be2 and castle. Avoid 6.Bb5?, which runs into ...Nxe5.
Surprise weapon: the Milner-Barry Gambit, 6.Bd3. It is risky against best play, but Black often grabs too much: 7...Nxd4?? loses the queen, and 10...Qxe5 11.Re1 sets more traps.

courses.repertoire: 3...c5 against the Advance, the Rubinstein (3...dxe4), and ...Nc6 in the Exchange
courses.summary: Build the ...e6 and ...d5 center, attack d4 against the Advance, take on e4 against 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2, and develop actively in the Exchange.
overview: The French idea: ...e6 and ...d5 build a solid center and keep f7 safe. The price is the c8 bishop behind your pawn on e6, so plan to free it or trade it.
The Exchange is your most common opponent, about three games in ten, because 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 exd5 4.d4 leads there too. Develop with ...Nc6, ...Bd6, ...Bg4, ...Qd7 and ...Nge7, and castle short.
Against the Advance (3.e5), about one game in five, hit d4 at once with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Against 6.a3, lock the queenside with 6...c4.
Against 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2, take on e4 (the Rubinstein): ...Nd7, ...Ngf6, then ...c5 to free your game.
In the Milner-Barry Gambit (6.Bd3), play ...Bd7 before ...Nxd4. Otherwise 8.Nxd4 Qxd4 9.Bb5+ wins your queen.
Against the Monte Carlo (4.c4), check with 4...Bb4+, castle, and take on c4 only after White's bishop has moved.

courses.repertoire: Exchange QGD and the minority attack, with 3.e3 against the Accepted
courses.summary: Take on d5 against the Declined and play the minority attack, meet the Slav with Nf3 and Nc3, and win the pawn back at once with 3.e3 against the Accepted.
overview: Against 2...e6, a third of your games, play 3.Nc3 and take at once: 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5. Follow with Qc2, e3, Bd3 and Nge2, and castle short.
The plan is the minority attack: Rb1, b4 and b5 leave Black with a weak pawn on c6 or d5. With the knight on e2, f3 and e4 is the second plan.
Don't grab d5 while Black's knight is on d7: 6.Nxd5?? Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ wins a piece for Black. This is the Elephant trap.
Against the Slav (2...c6), a quarter of your games, play 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3. Against 4...e6, take on d5 and play Bg5, the same plan as in the Exchange. Against an early ...Bf5, cxd5 and Qb3 hit b7.
Against the Accepted, play 3.e3 and win the pawn back with Bxc4. If Black holds it with 3...b5, a4 breaks the chain, and after 4...c6 5.axb5 cxb5, 6.Qf3 hits the rook on a8 and wins a piece.
Against 2...Nf6, one game in nine, take on d5: Black can't recapture with a pawn. Against the Albin (2...e5), play 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3, never 4.e3?, which runs into the Lasker trap.

courses.summary: Hold d5 with ...e6, castle quickly and play the Tartakower: ...h6, ...b6 and ...Bb7, then free the game with ...c5.
overview: Hold d5 with 2...e6, then ...Nf6, ...Be7 and castle. Against 4.Bg5, White's most common move, play the Tartakower: ...h6, ...b6 and ...Bb7.
Answer Bg5 with ...h6. If White takes on f6, take back with the bishop and keep the pawns in front of your king intact.

When White takes on d5 (8.cxd5, four games in ten), take back with the knight and trade pieces. Then ...Be6 and ...c5; after dxc5, take back with the b-pawn, and your hanging pawns on c5 and d5 are active.
Take on c4 only after White's bishop has left f1, so that Bxc4 costs White a tempo.
Against the Exchange (4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5), play 5...Nbd7, then ...c6, ...Be7, castle, ...Re8 and ...Nf8. White plays 6.Nxd5?? in one game in five, and it loses a piece to the Elephant trap.
Against 3.Nf3 and the Catalan (4.g3), play ...Be7 and castle, then take on c4 once White has castled. Follow with ...a6, then ...b5 and ...Bb7, or ...Bd7 and ...Bc6 if White stops ...b5 with a4.

surveys.name: Replies to 1.e4
surveys.subtitle: The six main openings after 1.e4, each played out to move 4, plus a page for the rarer ones.
surveys.summary:
After 1.e4, Black's main replies are 1...e5, 1...c5, 1...e6, 1...c6 and 1...d5. 1...e5 leads to the Open Games, where White's third move usually chooses between the Italian and the Ruy Lopez. 1...c5 fights for d4 from the side, 1...e6 and 1...c6 prepare ...d5, and 1...d5 challenges e4 at once.

Each board shows the position after four moves of a main line. Press Watch to see the moves played out. Under each board, three lines give White's plan and three give Black's. The Italian, French and Caro-Kann link to their courses in this app. Rarer openings, such as the Pirc and the King's Gambit, have a page of their own, linked at the bottom.

surveys.name: Uncommon replies to 1.e4
surveys.subtitle: The Pirc, King's Gambit, Scotch, Petroff, Modern and Alekhine, each played out to move 4.
surveys.summary:
Each of these openings comes up in fewer than 4 of every 100 games that start with 1.e4. They are listed from most to least common on Lichess (rated rapid and classical games, players averaging 1800 to 2199): the Pirc 3.7%, King's Gambit 3.4%, Scotch 3.1%, Petroff 2.8%, Modern 2.4% and Alekhine 1.4%. Three of them start with 1...e5: in the King's Gambit and the Scotch, White chooses the opening; in the Petroff, Black does.

Each board shows the position after four moves of a main line. Press Watch to see the moves played out. Under each board, three lines give White's plan and three give Black's.

surveys.name: Replies to 1.d4
surveys.subtitle: The Queen's Gambit, the Indian Defenses, and the other main replies.
surveys.summary: 1.d4 usually leads to slower, more strategic games than 1.e4. Black usually answers with 1...d5, which White meets with the Queen's Gambit, or with 1...Nf6, the start of the Indian Defenses. Instead of 2.c4, White can also meet 1...d5 with a system such as the London or the Colle: the same setup in almost every game, so they are easy to remember. The London is one of the most popular choices at club level (and works against 1...Nf6 too); the Colle is much rarer. The Queen's Gambit and the Indian Defenses each have their own page.

surveys.name: Queen's Gambit
surveys.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4: the main ways to decline it or take the pawn.
surveys.summary: White offers the c-pawn to lure Black's d-pawn away from the center. Black declines with 2...e6 or 2...c6, or takes it with 2...dxc4. The map shows how the variations branch, and the courses below teach a full repertoire for each side.

surveys.name: Indian Defenses
surveys.subtitle: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4: the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld, Queen's Indian and Benoni.
surveys.summary: Black develops the knight first and keeps the choice of setup open: fianchetto with ...g6, pin with ...Bb4, or hit d4 with ...c5. The map shows where each defense starts.

surveys.name: Uncommon replies to 1.d4
surveys.subtitle: The Dutch Defense and the Budapest Gambit, each played out to move 4.
surveys.summary: Each of these comes up in fewer than 3 of every 100 games that start with 1.d4: the Dutch (1...f5) in about 2.6, the Budapest Gambit (1...Nf6 2.c4 e5) in about 1.3. Source: rated rapid and classical games on Lichess, players averaging 1800 to 2199. No course is planned for them yet.

surveys.name: Other first moves
surveys.subtitle: The five first moves you meet most besides 1.e4 and 1.d4, with Black's main replies, each played out to move 4.
surveys.summary:
On Lichess, 1.e4 starts 62% of games and 1.d4 26%. Next come 1.c4, the English (4%), and 1.Nf3, the Zukertort (3%). 1.f4, 1.b3 and 1.g3 each start about 1 game in 100. These openings attack the center from the side and develop quietly, so they often turn into a 1.d4 opening or the English.

Each opening has one board and a Watch button for each of Black's main replies, played out to move 4 along the moves club players choose most often on Lichess. Under each board, White's plan and Black's plan are summed up in a few lines.
